projects.title: Recover Published iOS App Code
projects.full_description:
An iOS app I own is live in the Apple App Store, yet the entire original project is missing—no repository access, no local backups, nothing at all. What I still hold is the production build that Apple distributes, plus my own App Store Connect credentials. 

The goal is to retrieve the app’s source code, or at least rebuild a functionally identical Xcode project that I can maintain going forward. Only the source code matters; all assets and configuration files are already in my possession through the binary and App Store metadata. 

Because there is zero existing codebase to pull from, the work will most likely involve decompiling and reverse-engineering the published binary. Familiarity with tools such as Hopper, Ghidra, IDA, or similar Objective-C/Swift decompilers will be essential, along with solid understanding of iOS frameworks, provisioning profiles, and Xcode project structure. 

Deliverables 
• A compilable Xcode project that reproduces the current App Store build’s functionality. 
• Clear build instructions so I can archive, sign, and upload future releases myself. 
• A brief technical report outlining the reverse-engineering approach, any third-party libraries identified, and areas where source parity could not be reached (if any). 

Acceptance criteria 
• The rebuilt app installs on a test device and matches the live version’s features and UI flow. 
• Apple’s App Store Connect validation passes with no new warnings beyond those in the existing binary. 

Feel free to suggest the most efficient path—whether straight binary decompilation, partial rewriting after interface extraction, or another method you’ve proven effective. Confidentiality and adherence to Apple’s policies are, of course, non-negotiable.

projects.title: PLA Prototype to Manufacture-Ready Rigid Shell + Silicone Overmold
projects.full_description:
Mechanical/Product Design Engineer — PLA Prototype to Manufacture-Ready Rigid Shell + Silicone Overmold

Overview

We have a working 3D-printed (PLA) prototype of a small electronics case with an internal sliding compartment, custom PCB, embedded magnet, and Hall-effect sensor. We need a mechanical/product design engineer to redesign it into a manufacture-ready rigid shell with a silicone overmold, and deliver a finished, consumer-presentable prototype for user testing.

What we need done

Redesign for manufacturing (DFM): Convert the existing case into mold-ready CAD — a rigid inner shell housing the PCB, battery, magnet, and sensor, and forming the sliding compartment mechanism, plus a silicone overmold over the exterior for grip, shock absorption, and water resistance (leaving the moving compartment free of overmold). Include proper wall thickness, draft angles, mounting bosses, and undercuts for a secure silicone bond.
Material and process spec: Document the recommended rigid substrate material, silicone/LSR grade and hardness (Shore A), and bonding method — clear enough to hand directly to a manufacturer for quoting.
Manufacture-ready files: Final CAD in native and neutral formats (e.g., STEP), with separate parts for the rigid shell and overmold, ready to submit to an injection molder (e.g., Protolabs, Xometry, Fictiv, or an overseas manufacturer).
Finished prototype: A working unit (or small batch, ideally 3–5) with the rigid-shell-and-overmold construction and our existing electronics integrated. The final product must be genuinely consumer-ready in look and feel for hands-on user testing. For this project—a phone case—it is critical that the delivered product is finalized as "one-and-done," requiring no further iterations or adjustments after delivery.

What we're looking for

Proven experience designing plastic/rubber parts for injection molding and overmolding specifically (not just general CAD work) — please share examples of past projects where you took a design through this exact rigid-plus-silicone-overmold process.
Comfort working with small mechanical assemblies (sliding/drawer mechanisms, embedded magnets, PCB mounting) inside a consumer electronics enclosure.
Ability to either produce the physical prototype yourself or manage sourcing it through a rapid-prototyping manufacturer (Protolabs/Xometry/Fictiv or similar) on our behalf.
Clear, organized documentation habits — we need the process spec to be something we can hand to a factory later without you in the room.
